claim: Formicine ants actively swallow their antimicrobial, highly acidic poison gland secretion.
source: Here we show that formicine ants actively swallow their antimicrobial, highly acidic poison gland secretion.
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing crop pH changes and prevention experiments.

claim: The crop of C. floridanus becomes increasingly acidic over time after feeding, reaching highly acidic values 48 hr after feeding (median pH = 2; 95% CI: 1.5–3.4).
source: We found that after feeding the crop became increasingly acidic over time, reaching highly acidic values 48 hr after feeding (median pH = 2; 95% CI: 1.5–3.4)
evidence: Supported by pH measurements at different time points after feeding, shown in Figure 1a.

claim: Crop pH levels of C. floridanus ants were highly acidic in workers taken directly out of a satiated colony (major workers: median pH = 2, 95% CI: 2–3; minor workers: median pH = 3, CI: 2.5–3.6).
source: We also found that crop pH levels of C. floridanus ants were highly acidic in workers taken directly out of a satiated colony (Figure 1—figure supplement 1; major workers: median pH = 2, 95% CI: 2–3; minor workers: median pH = 3, CI: 2.5–3.6)
evidence: Supported by pH measurements from colony workers, shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Under natural conditions an acidic baseline pH in the crop lumen is maintained following perturbation through ingested fluids.
source: suggesting that under natural conditions an acidic baseline pH in the crop lumen is maintained following perturbation thereof through ingested fluids.
evidence: Inferred from pH measurements in satiated and starved workers showing consistently acidic pH.

claim: Prevention of acidopore grooming in C. floridanus ants significantly diminished crop acidity compared to ants that were not prevented from acidopore grooming.
source: This experiment revealed that acidopore grooming prevented ants showed a significantly diminished acidity in their crop compared to ants that were not prevented from acidopore grooming (Figure 1b; LMM, LR-test, χ2 = 44.68, df = 1, p<0.001).
evidence: Supported by experimental manipulation preventing acidopore grooming and pH measurements, shown in Figure 1b.

claim: A similar, significantly diminished acidity in crop lumens was ubiquitously obtained in a comparative survey across seven formicine ant species and three genera upon prevention of acidopore grooming.
source: A similar, significantly diminished acidity in crop lumens was ubiquitously obtained in a comparative survey across seven formicine ant species and three genera (Camponotus, Lasius, and Formica) upon comparison of ants that were prevented from acidopore grooming through immobilization to non-prevented ants (Figure 1c; two-sided Wilcoxon rank-sum tests, comparisons for all ant species: p≤0.036).
evidence: Supported by comparative pH measurements across multiple species, shown in Figure 1c.

claim: Formicine ants attain a highly acidic baseline pH in their crop lumen by taking up their poison into their mouth during acidopore grooming and subsequently swallowing it.
source: We conclude that formicine ants attain a highly acidic baseline pH in their crop lumen by taking up their poison into their mouth during acidopore grooming (Tragust et al., 2013), and subsequently swallowing it.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from experimental data showing prevention of acidopore grooming reduces crop acidity, and citation to previous work on poison uptake behavior.

claim: Swallowing of the poison is widespread among formicine ants.
source: The comparative survey also shows that this behavior is widespread among formicine ants.
evidence: Supported by comparative data across seven formicine ant species from three genera.

claim: C. floridanus ants increase the frequency of acidopore grooming within the first 30 min after ingesting fluids compared to unfed ants irrespective of the fluid's nutritional value.
source: We also found that C. floridanus ants increase the frequency of acidopore grooming within the first 30 min after ingesting fluids compared to unfed ants irrespective of the fluid's nutritional value (Figure 1—figure supplement 2; GLMM, LR-test, χ2 = 33.526, df = 2, p<0.001; Westfall corrected post-hoc pairwise comparisons, water versus. 10% honey-water: p=0.634, unfed versus water and unfed versus 10% honey-water: both p<0.001).
evidence: Supported by behavioral observations and statistical analysis, shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: The strong acidity was limited to the crop of C. floridanus ants and did not extend to the midgut.
source: Moreover, we found that the strong acidity was limited to the crop of C. floridanus ants and did not extend to the midgut, the primary site of digestion in insects (Holtof et al., 2019; Terra and Ferreira, 1994; Figure 1—figure supplement 3; pH-measurements at four points along the midgut 24 hr after access to 10% honey-water; mean ± se; midgut position 1 = 5.08 ± 0.18, midgut position 2 = 5.28 ± 0.17, midgut position 3 = 5.43 ± 0.16, midgut position 4 = 5.31 ± 0.19).
evidence: Supported by pH measurements at multiple positions along the digestive tract, shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3, and citations to literature on insect digestion.

claim: Poison acidified crop lumens in formicine ants may serve microbial control, limiting infection by oral pathogens.
source: Together, these results led us to hypothesize that poison acidified crop lumens in formicine ants do not primarily serve a digestive function but may serve microbial control, limiting infection by oral pathogens.
evidence: Hypothesis based on inference from experimental data showing acidic crop pH and its localization.

claim: Only a small amount of ingested food is passed from the crop to the midgut 2–4 hr after feeding in C. floridanus, while thereafter food is steadily passed from the crop to the midgut until 18 hr after feeding.
source: In agreement with food passage times through the gastrointestinal tract of other ants (Cannon, 1998; Kloft, 1960b; Kloft, 1960a; Howard and Tschinkel, 1981; Markin, 1970), we found that only a small amount of ingested food is passed from the crop to the midgut 2–4 hr after feeding, while thereafter food is steadily passed from the crop to the midgut until 18 hr after feeding (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by fluorescent particle tracking data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1, and citations to literature on ant food passage.

claim: S. marcescens presence decreased sharply over time in the crop of C. floridanus after ingestion with food.
source: We found that S. marcescens presence decreased sharply over time in the crop (Figure 2a; GLMM, LR-test, χ2 = 220.78, df = 4, p<0.001).
evidence: Supported by bacterial viability measurements in the crop over time, shown in Figure 2a.

claim: The proportion of S. marcescens CFUs retrieved from the crop relative to the mean at 0 hr diminished from 43% at 0.5 hr post-feeding to 0% at 4 hr, 24 hr, and 48 hr post-feeding.
source: The proportion of CFUs that we were able to retrieve from the crop relative to the mean at 0 hr in the crop diminished from 43% at 0.5 hr post-feeding (median, CI: 0–543%) to 0% at 4 hr (CI: 0–4%), 24 hr (CI: 0–1.8%), and 48 hr (CI: 0–18%) post-feeding.
evidence: Supported by quantitative bacterial viability data from crop measurements.

claim: S. marcescens could only be detected at extremely low numbers in the midgut relative to the mean at 0 hr in the crop, and not at all at 4 hr and 48 hr post-feeding.
source: In addition, relative to the mean at 0 hr in the crop, S. marcescens could only be detected at extremely low numbers in the midgut (median 0%) at 0 hr (CI: 0–4%), 0.5 hr (CI: 0–1%) and 24 hr (CI: 0–1%) post-feeding and not at all at 4 hr and 48 hr post-feeding (Figure 2b; GLMM, LR-test, χ2 = 1.044, df = 2, p=0.593).
evidence: Supported by bacterial viability measurements in the midgut over time, shown in Figure 2b.

claim: A similar, rapid reduction in the crop and inability to pass from the crop to the midgut was obtained when E. coli was fed to C. floridanus ants.
source: A similar, rapid reduction in the crop and inability to pass from the crop to the midgut was obtained when we fed E. coli, a potential opportunistic bacterium that is not a gut associate of insects (Blount, 2015) to C. floridanus ants (Figure 2—figure supplement 2; crop: GLMM, LR-test, χ2 = 156.74, df = 4, p<0.001; midgut: GLMM, LR-test, χ2 = 14.898, df = 3, p=0.002).
evidence: Supported by bacterial viability measurements with E. coli shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2, and citation about E. coli not being an insect gut associate.

claim: Incubation of S. marcescens for 2 hr in 10% honey water acidified with formic acid to pH 4 resulted in a significantly lower number of CFUs relative to pH 5 and in zero growth for incubations at pH-levels lower than 4.
source: We found that incubation of S. marcescens for 2 hr in 10% honey water acidified with formic acid to pH 4 resulted in a significantly lower number of CFUs relative to pH 5 and in zero growth for incubations at pH-levels that were lower than 4 (Figure 2—figure supplement 3; GLM, LR-test, χ2 = 79.442, df = 1, p<0.001).
evidence: Supported by in vitro bacterial growth assay data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3.

claim: Poison acidified crops can serve microbial control in formicine ants, likely inhibiting bacteria according to their ability to cope with acidic environments.
source: Our data thus indicate that poison acidified crops can indeed serve microbial control in formicine ants, likely inhibiting bacteria according to their ability to cope with acidic environments (Lund et al., 2014).
evidence: Conclusion inferred from in vivo and in vitro bacterial viability data, with citation to literature on bacterial acid tolerance.

claim: Acidopore access after pathogen ingestion significantly increased the survival probability of C. floridanus ants.
source: We found that acidopore access after pathogen ingestion significantly increased the survival probability of ants (Figure 3; COXME, LR-test, χ2 = 20.95, df = 3, p=0.0001).
evidence: Supported by survival experiment data shown in Figure 3.

claim: The survival of ants prevented from acidopore grooming and fed once with pathogen contaminated food was significantly lower than that of non-prevented ants fed the same food source.
source: The survival of ants prevented from acidopore grooming and fed once with the pathogen contaminated food was significantly lower than that of non-prevented ants fed the same food source (Westfall corrected post-hoc comparisons: FA - | Serratia presence + versus. all other ant groups: p≤0.027).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of survival experiment data.

claim: Non-prevented ants fed once with pathogen contaminated food did not differ in survival to prevented and non-prevented ants fed non-contaminated food.
source: In contrast, non-prevented ants fed once with the pathogen contaminated food source did not differ in survival to prevented and non-prevented ants fed the non-contaminated food source (Westfall corrected post-hoc comparisons: FA + | Serratia presence + versus. FA + | Serratia presence – and FA + | Serratia presence + versus. FA + | Serratia presence –: p≥0.061 for both comparisons).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of survival experiment data.

claim: Poison acidified crop lumens provide a fitness benefit in terms of survival to formicine ants upon ingestion of pathogen contaminated food.
source: this result indicates that poison acidified crop lumens provide a fitness benefit in terms of survival to formicine ants upon ingestion of pathogen contaminated food.
evidence: Conclusion inferred from survival experiment results.

claim: The duration of trophallaxis between donor-receiver ant pairs during the first 30 min of the first feeding bout did not significantly differ between pairs with blocked and unblocked donor ants.
source: We found that the duration of trophallaxis between the two donor-receiver ant pairs during the first 30 min. of the first feeding bout did not significantly differ (Figure 4—figure supplement 1; LMM, LR-test, χ2 = 1.23, df = 1, p=0.268)
evidence: Supported by behavioral observation data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Trophallactic behavior was not influenced through acidopore blockage in donor ants at the beginning of the experiment.
source: indicating that trophallactic behavior was not influenced through acidopore blockage in donor ants at the beginning of the experiment.
evidence: Inferred from the lack of significant difference in trophallaxis duration between treatment groups.

claim: Acidopore blockage per se had a significant negative effect on the survival of donor as well as receiver ants.
source: Over the next 12 d, we found that acidopore blockage per se had a significant negative effect on the survival of donor as well as receiver ants (Figure 4; COXME, LR-test, χ2 = 66.68, df = 3, p<0.001).
evidence: Supported by survival data from donor-receiver ant pairs shown in Figure 4.

claim: Receiver ants that obtained food from donors with the ability to swallow the poison died at a higher rate than their respective donor counterparts (hazard ratio: 1.81).
source: However, although receiver ants that obtained food every other day from donors with the ability to swallow the poison died at a higher rate than their respective donor counterparts (hazard ratio: 1.81; Westfall corrected post-hoc comparison: p<0.001)
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of survival data from donor-receiver pairs.

claim: Receiver ants that obtained pathogen contaminated food from donors with the ability to swallow poison were only half as likely to die compared to receiver ants that obtained food from blocked donors unable to swallow their poison (hazard ratio: 0.56).
source: they were only half as likely to die compared to receiver ants that obtained pathogen contaminated food from blocked donors unable to swallow their poison (hazard ratio: 0.56; Westfall corrected post-hoc comparison: p<0.001).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of survival data from donor-receiver pairs.

claim: Swallowing of the poison and the ensuing crop acidity provides a fitness benefit to other members of a formicine ant society.
source: This indicates that swallowing of the poison and the ensuing crop acidity also provides a fitness benefit to other members of a formicine ant society.
evidence: Conclusion inferred from survival data of receiver ants in trophallaxis experiments.

claim: Asaia sp. was not affected by an incubation for 2 hr in 10% honey water acidified with formic acid to pH 4 and was still able to grow when incubated at pH 3 in in vitro tests.
source: In contrast to S. marcescens (Figure 2—figure supplement 2), Asaia sp. was not affected by an incubation for 2 hr in 10% honey water acidified with formic acid to pH 4 and was still able to grow when incubated at pH 3 in in vitro tests (Figure 5—figure supplement 1; GLM, overall LR-test χ2 = 21.179, df = 2, p<0.001; Westfall corrected post hoc comparisons: pH = 5 versus. pH = 4: p=0.234, all other comparisons: p<0.001).
evidence: Supported by in vitro bacterial growth assay data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: Asaia sp. only gradually diminished over time in the crop with the proportion of CFUs retrieved from the crop relative to the mean at 0 hr diminishing to only 34% at 4 hr and 2% at 24 hr post-feeding.
source: Moreover, in in vivo tests, Asaia sp. only gradually diminished over time in the crop (Figure 5a; GLMM; LR-test, χ2 = 124.01, df = 4, p<0.001) with the proportion of CFUs that we were able to retrieve from the crop relative to the mean at 0 hr in the crop diminishing to only 34% (median, CI: 3–85%) and 2% (CI: 0–7%) at 4 hr and 24 hr post-feeding, respectively.
evidence: Supported by in vivo bacterial viability measurements in the crop shown in Figure 5a.

claim: Asaia sp. steadily increased in the midgut from its initial absence at 0 hr post-feeding to 2% at 48 hr post-feeding relative to the mean at 0 hr in the crop.
source: At the same time, relative to the mean at 0 hr in the crop, Asaia sp. steadily increased in the midgut (Figure 5b; GLMM; LR-test, χ2 = 59.94, df = 3, p<0.001) from its initial absence at 0 hr post-feeding to 2% (median, CI: 0–5%) at 48 hr post-feeding.
evidence: Supported by in vivo bacterial viability measurements in the midgut shown in Figure 5b.

claim: In formicine ants, poison acidified crops might act as a chemical filter that works selectively against the establishment of opportunistic and potentially harmful bacteria but allows entry and establishment of members of the bacterial family Acetobacteraceae.
source: This suggests that in formicine ants, poison acidified crops might act as a chemical filter that works selectively against the establishment of opportunistic and potentially harmful bacteria but allows entry and establishment of members of the bacterial family Acetobacteraceae.
evidence: Conclusion inferred from differential survival and passage of Asaia sp. versus S. marcescens and E. coli through the crop.

claim: Highly acidic stomach lumens are ubiquitous in higher vertebrates, including amphibians, reptiles, birds and mammals.
source: Highly acidic stomach lumens are ubiquitous in higher vertebrates, including amphibians, reptiles, birds and mammals (Beasley et al., 2015; Koelz, 1992).
evidence: Supported by citations to literature on vertebrate stomach acidity.

claim: In insects, highly acidic gut regions have so far only rarely been described from the midgut.
source: In insects, highly acidic gut regions have so far only rarely been described from the midgut (Chapman, 2013; Holtof et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to literature on insect gut pH.

claim: The mechanisms responsible for the creation of a gut lumen compartment with a certain pH are often unknown in insects.
source: The mechanisms responsible for the creation of a gut lumen compartment with a certain pH are often unknown in insects (Harrison, 2001)
evidence: Supported by citation to literature on insect gut physiology.

claim: Highly acidic gut regions in insects may be generated through physiological mechanisms similar to vertebrates.
source: but in principle, highly acidic gut regions in insects may, similar to vertebrates (Hersey and Sachs, 1995), be generated through physiological mechanisms (Matthews, 2017; Miguel-Aliaga et al., 2018; Onken and Moffett, 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to literature on vertebrate and insect gut physiology.

claim: Acidic derivatives of gut-associated microbes might contribute to the insect gut pH.
source: Alternatively, acidic derivatives of gut-associated microbes (Ratzke et al., 2018, Ratzke and Gore, 2018, Wolfe, 2005) or acidic gland secretions (Blum, 1996; Morgan, 2008; Vander Meer, 2012) might contribute to the insect gut pH.
evidence: Supported by citations to literature on microbial metabolites and gland secretions.

claim: Sanitation of food through the addition of organic acids or through acidic fermentation is frequently practiced by humans.
source: Sanitation of food through the addition of organic acids or through acidic fermentation is frequently practiced by humans (Cherrington et al., 1991; Hirshfield et al., 2003; Theron and Rykers Lues, 2010)
evidence: Supported by citations to literature on human food preservation practices.

claim: Sanitation of food with antimicrobials from different sources is ubiquitous in animals that provision food to their offspring or that store, cultivate, develop or live in food.
source: and sanitation of food with antimicrobials from different sources is ubiquitous in animals that provision food to their offspring or that store, cultivate, develop or live in food (Currie et al., 1999; Herzner et al., 2013; Herzner and Strohm, 2007; Joop et al., 2014; Mueller et al., 2005; Vander Wall, 1990).
evidence: Supported by citations to literature on antimicrobial use in various animal species.

claim: A microbial control function of poison acidified crops in formicine ants to sanitize ingested food is supported by survival experiments and bacterial growth and viability experiments.
source: A microbial control function of poison acidified crops in formicine ants to sanitize ingested food is supported by our survival experiments and our in vivo and in vitro bacterial growth and viability experiments.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from multiple experimental results presented in the study.

claim: Access to the poison improved survival of formicine ants after feeding on pathogen contaminated food.
source: There we found that access to the poison improved survival of formicine ants after feeding on pathogen contaminated food.
evidence: Supported by survival experiment data.

claim: Pathogenic and opportunistic bacteria were quickly inhibited in the crop when ingested with food and could not establish in the midgut.
source: We also found that pathogenic and opportunistic bacteria were quickly inhibited in the crop when ingested with food and could not establish in the midgut.
evidence: Supported by bacterial viability and growth experiment data.

claim: It is unclear whether the acidic environment in the crop is sufficient to protect formicine ants and to inhibit pathogenic and opportunistic microbes ingested with food or whether acidic conditions act in concert with other factors.
source: At present it is unclear whether the acidic environment in the crop is sufficient to protect formicine ants and to inhibit pathogenic and opportunistic microbes ingested with food or whether acidic conditions act in concert with other factors.
evidence: Statement of uncertainty about mechanisms, acknowledging limitations of current data.

claim: Studies in vertebrates and Drosophila melanogaster have shown that acidic gut regions together with immune system effectors serve microbial control and prevent infection by oral pathogens.
source: Studies in vertebrates and the fruit fly Drosophila melanogaster have shown that acidic gut regions together with immune system effectors serve microbial control and prevent infection by oral pathogens (Giannella et al., 1972; Howden and Hunt, 1987; Martinsen et al., 2005; Overend et al., 2016; Rakoff-Nahoum et al., 2004; Slack et al., 2009; Tennant et al., 2008; Watnick and Jugder, 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to literature on gut immunity in vertebrates and Drosophila.

claim: Previous studies investigating formicine ant trophallactic fluids found the presence of proteins related to cathepsin D, a lysosomal aspartic protease that can exhibit antibacterial effector activity and the proteolytic production of antimicrobial peptides.
source: Concordantly, previous studies investigating formicine ant trophallactic fluids Hamilton et al., 2011; LeBoeuf et al., 2016 found the presence of proteins related to cathepsin D, a lysosomal aspartic protease that can exhibit antibacterial effector activity and the proteolytic production of antimicrobial peptides (Ning et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies on ant trophallactic fluids and cathepsin D function.

claim: The ability of donor ants to access their poison improved the survival of receiver ants without access to their poison following trophallactic exchange of pathogen-contaminated food.
source: In addition to improving their own survival, the ability of donor ants to access their poison also improved the survival of receiver ants without access to their poison following trophallactic exchange of pathogen-contaminated food.
evidence: Supported by survival data from donor-receiver ant pair experiments.

claim: Acidic crop lumens might act as a barrier to disease spread in formicine ant societies, alleviating the cost of sharing pathogen contaminated food.
source: Acidic crop lumens might therefore act as a barrier to disease spread in formicine ant societies, alleviating the cost of sharing pathogen contaminated food (Onchuru et al., 2018; Salem et al., 2015)
evidence: Conclusion inferred from trophallaxis experiment results, with citations to literature on costs of food sharing.

claim: Acidic crop lumens counteract the generally increased risk of pathogen exposure and transmission associated with group-living.
source: and counteracting the generally increased risk of pathogen exposure and transmission associated with group-living (Alexander, 1974; Boomsma et al., 2005; Kappeler et al., 2015).
evidence: Conclusion inferred from experimental results, with citations to literature on disease risks in social groups.

claim: Host filtering of microbes via acidic crop lumens might explain at least part of the recurrent presence of Acetobacteraceae in the gut of formicine ants and the otherwise reduced microbial diversity and abundance of gut-associated microbes in formicine ants.
source: This suggests that host filtering of microbes (Mazel et al., 2018) via acidic crop lumens might explain at least part of the recurrent presence of Acetobacteraceae in the gut of formicine ants and the otherwise reduced microbial diversity and abundance of gut-associated microbes in formicine ants (Brown and Wernegreen, 2016; Brown and Wernegreen, 2019; Chua et al., 2018; Chua et al., 2020; Ivens et al., 2018; Russell et al., 2017).
evidence: Conclusion inferred from differential bacterial survival data, with citations to literature on host filtering and formicine ant microbiota.

claim: Recent studies indicate a mutualistic relationship between formicine ants and their gut-associated Acetobacteraceae.
source: Though not formally established (see Mushegian and Ebert, 2016), recent studies indicate a mutualistic relationship between formicine ants, and their gut-associated Acetobacteraceae (Brown and Wernegreen, 2019; Chua et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to recent literature on ant-Acetobacteraceae interactions, with acknowledgment of uncertainty.

claim: The creation of an acidic crop environment in formicine ants that is easier to endure if colonizing microbes are mutualists agrees with the concept of screening as a mechanism to choose microbial partners.
source: Thus, the creation of an acidic crop environment in formicine ants that is easier to endure if colonizing microbes are mutualists agrees with the concept of screening as a mechanism to choose microbial partners out of a pool of environmental microbes (Archetti et al., 2011a; Archetti et al., 2011b; Biedermann and Kaltenpoth, 2014; Scheuring and Yu, 2012).
evidence: Conclusion inferred from experimental results, with citations to literature on screening mechanisms in symbiosis.

claim: In screening, a costly environment is imposed on partners that excludes all but high-quality ones.
source: Contrary to signalling, where costly information is displayed to partners, in screening a costly environment is imposed on partners that excludes all but high-quality ones.
evidence: Definition of screening mechanism from established theory.

claim: Partner choice in a number of cross-kingdom mutualisms is readily explained by screening.
source: Partner choice in a number of cross-kingdom mutualisms is readily explained by screening (see examples in Archetti et al., 2011a; Archetti et al., 2011b; Biedermann and Kaltenpoth, 2014; Scheuring and Yu, 2012)
evidence: Supported by citations to literature on screening in various mutualisms.

claim: Experimental evidence for screening is so far limited in insect-microbe associations.
source: but experimental evidence is so far limited in insect-microbe associations (Innocent et al., 2018; Itoh et al., 2019; Ranger et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to limited literature on experimental evidence for screening in insect-microbe systems.

claim: The results of this study would provide support for the prediction that screening is more likely to evolve from a host's defense trait against parasites.
source: Although our experiments can only hint at screening as a means of partner choice in formicine ants, the results of our study would provide support for the prediction that screening is more likely to evolve from a host's defense trait against parasites (Archetti et al., 2011a; Archetti et al., 2011b), that is, the highly acidic, antimicrobial poison that creates a selective environment for microbes.
evidence: Conclusion inferred from experimental results, with citations to theoretical predictions about screening evolution.

claim: This study might provide evidence that the well-established cross talk between the immune system and gut-associated microbes in vertebrates and invertebrates can hold for a broader range of immune defense traits.
source: Our study might therefore not only provide evidence that the well-established cross talk between the immune system and gut-associated microbes in vertebrates and invertebrates (Chu and Mazmanian, 2013; Rakoff-Nahoum et al., 2004; Slack et al., 2009; Watnick and Jugder, 2020; Xiao et al., 2019) can hold for a broader range of immune defense traits (sensu Otti et al., 2014)
evidence: Conclusion inferred from study results, with citations to literature on immune-microbe interactions and defense traits.

claim: The cross talk between immune defense traits and gut-associated microbes can be realized through signals and through screening.
source: but also that this cross talk can be realized through signals (Fischbach and Segre, 2016; Moura-Alves et al., 2019; Villena et al., 2018) and through screening.
evidence: Conclusion inferred from study results, with citations to literature on signaling mechanisms.

claim: Poison acidified crop lumens of formicine ants can act as a chemical filter for control and selection of microbes ingested with food.
source: Overall, our study provides evidence that poison acidified crop lumens of formicine ants can act as a chemical filter for control and selection of microbes ingested with food.
evidence: Summary conclusion drawn from all experimental results presented in the study.

claim: Poison acidified formicine crops might contribute to the ecological and evolutionary success of this group of insects by alleviating the increased risk of pathogen exposure and transmission associated with group living but allowing the acquisition and transmission of microbial mutualists.
source: Poison acidified formicine crops might thus contribute to the ecological and evolutionary success of this group of insects by alleviating the increased risk of pathogen exposure and transmission associated with group living but allowing the acquisition and transmission of microbial mutualists.
evidence: Speculative conclusion about broader implications, inferred from experimental results.

claim: Similar microbial filters likely represent a widespread theme to manage harmful and beneficial host-associated microbes but have so far only partly been uncovered in a few animal systems.
source: Similar microbial filters likely represent a widespread theme to manage harmful and beneficial host-associated microbes but have so far only partly been uncovered in a few animal systems (Cardoza et al., 2006; Duarte et al., 2018; Sapountzis et al., 2019; Scott et al., 2008; Shukla et al., 2018a; Shukla et al., 2018b; Vogel et al., 2017).
evidence: Speculative conclusion about broader patterns, with citations to literature on microbial filters in other systems.

claim: Animals commonly harbor gut-associated microbial communities.
source: Animals commonly harbor gut-associated microbial communities (Engel and Moran, 2013; Moran et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to literature on animal gut microbiomes.

claim: Patterns of recurring gut microbial communities have been described for many animal groups.
source: Patterns of recurring gut microbial communities have been described for many animal groups (Brune and Dietrich, 2015; Kwong et al., 2017; Ochman et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to literature on gut microbiome patterns across taxa.

claim: The processes generating patterns of recurring gut microbial communities are often not well understood.
source: The processes generating these patterns are however often not well understood.
evidence: Statement about current state of knowledge in the field.

claim: Patterns of recurring gut microbial communities might result from host filtering.
source: They might result from host filtering (Mazel et al., 2018)
evidence: Supported by citation to literature on host filtering mechanisms.

claim: Patterns of recurring gut microbial communities might result from a shared evolutionary history between gut-associated microbes and their hosts involving microbial adaptations to the host environment.
source: a shared evolutionary history between gut-associated microbes and their hosts (Moeller et al., 2016) involving microbial adaptations to the host environment (McFall-Ngai et al., 2013)
evidence: Supported by citations to literature on coevolution and microbial adaptation.

claim: Patterns of recurring gut microbial communities might simply be a byproduct of similar host dietary preferences.
source: simply be a byproduct of similar host dietary preferences (Anderson et al., 2012; Hammer et al., 2017)
evidence: Supported by citations to literature on diet and microbiome composition.

claim: Patterns of recurring gut microbial communities might result from interactions between microbes in the gut-associated microbial community.
source: or result from interactions between microbes in the gut-associated microbial community (Brinker et al., 2019; García-Bayona and Comstock, 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to literature on microbial interactions.

claim: Food is an important environmental source of microbial gut associates.
source: Food is an important environmental source of microbial gut associates (Blum et al., 2013; Broderick and Lemaitre, 2012; David et al., 2014; Hammer et al., 2017; Perez-Cobas et al., 2015; Pais et al., 2018)
evidence: Supported by citations to literature on food as a source of gut microbes.

claim: Food poses a challenge to discriminate between harmful and beneficial microbes, as food may contain microbes that produce toxic chemicals or that are pathogenic.
source: but also poses a challenge, the need to discriminate between harmful and beneficial microbes, as food may contain microbes that produce toxic chemicals or that are pathogenic (Burkepile et al., 2006; Demain and Fang, 2000; Janzen, 1977; Trienens et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to literature on microbial toxins and pathogens in food.

claim: In social animals, control of harmful microbes in food while allowing the acquisition and transmission of beneficial microbes is likely especially important.
source: In social animals, control of harmful microbes in food while at the same time allowing the acquisition and transmission of beneficial microbes from and with food, is likely especially important.
evidence: Logical inference about the importance of microbial control in social species.

claim: Eusocial Hymenoptera transport and store food in their stomach, the crop.
source: Eusocial Hymenoptera not only transport and store food in their stomach, the crop
evidence: Statement of known biological fact about eusocial Hymenoptera.

claim: Eusocial Hymenoptera distribute food to members of their colony via trophallaxis.
source: but also distribute food to members of their colony via trophallaxis, i.e. the regurgitation of crop content from donor individuals to receiver individuals through mouth-to-mouth feeding (Gernat et al., 2018; Greenwald et al., 2018; LeBoeuf et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to literature on trophallaxis behavior.

claim: Trophallaxis can facilitate the transmission of beneficial microbes.
source: While trophallaxis can facilitate the transmission of beneficial microbes
evidence: Logical inference about potential benefits of trophallaxis.

claim: Trophallaxis can entail significant costs, as it might open the door to unwanted microbial opportunists and pathogens.
source: it can also entail significant costs, as it might open the door to unwanted microbial opportunists and pathogens that can take advantage of these transmission routes (Onchuru et al., 2018; Salem et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to literature on pathogen transmission via trophallaxis.

claim: Apart from specialized intracellular endosymbionts associated with the midgut in the ant tribe Camponotini, formicine ant species have only low abundances of microbial associates in their gut lumen.
source: Apart from specialized intracellular endosymbionts associated with the midgut in the ant tribe Camponotini (Degnan et al., 2004; Feldhaar et al., 2007; Russell et al., 2017; Williams and Wernegreen, 2015), formicine ant species have only low abundances of microbial associates in their gut lumen
evidence: Supported by citations to literature on formicine ant microbiota.

claim: Formicine ant species carry members of the bacterial family Acetobacteraceae as a recurring part of their gut microbiota.
source: but carry members of the bacterial family Acetobacteraceae as a recurring part of their gut microbiota (Brown and Wernegreen, 2016; Chua et al., 2018; He et al., 2011; Ivens et al., 2018; Russell et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to literature on Acetobacteraceae in formicine ants.

claim: Some formicine gut-associated Acetobacteraceae show signs of genomic and metabolic adaptations to their host environment indicating coevolution and mutual benefit.
source: Some formicine gut-associated Acetobacteraceae show signs of genomic and metabolic adaptations to their host environment indicating coevolution and mutual benefit (Brown and Wernegreen, 2019; Chua et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to literature on Acetobacteraceae adaptations.

claim: The recurrent presence of Acetobacteraceae in the gut of formicine ants potentially reflects direct transmission of bacteria among individuals, selective uptake on the part of the ants, specific adaptations for colonizing ant guts on the part of the bacteria, or some combination of all three.
source: But the recurrent presence of Acetobacteraceae in the gut of formicine ants potentially also reflects the direct transmission of bacteria among individuals, selective uptake on the part of the ants, specific adaptations for colonizing ant guts on the part of the bacteria, or some combination of all three (Engel and Moran, 2013).
evidence: Speculative statement about possible mechanisms, with citation to literature on insect-microbe associations.

claim: Formicine ant species possess a highly acidic poison gland secretion containing formic acid as its main component.
source: Formicine ant species possess a highly acidic poison gland secretion containing formic acid as its main component (Lopez et al., 1993; Osman and Brander, 1961; Schmidt, 1986).
evidence: Supported by citations to literature on formicine ant poison composition.

claim: The poison is presumably foremost used as a defensive weapon.
source: Although the poison is presumably foremost used as a defensive weapon (Osman and Kloft, 1961)
evidence: Supported by citation to literature on poison function.

claim: The poison is distributed to the environment of formicine ants as an external immune defense trait to protect their offspring and the nest and to limit disease spread within the society.
source: it is also distributed to the environment of these ants as an external immune defense trait (sensu Otti et al., 2014) to protect their offspring and the nest and to limit disease spread within the society (see references in Tragust, 2016; Brütsch et al., 2017; Pull et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to literature on external immune defense in ants.

claim: Ants take up their poison from the acidopore into their mouth during acidopore grooming.
source: To this end, ants take up their poison from the acidopore, the opening of the poison gland at the gaster tip, into their mouth (Tragust et al., 2013) during a specialized behavior existing only in a subset of ant families among all Hymenopterans (Basibuyuk and Quicke, 1999; Farish, 1972), termed acidopore grooming.
evidence: Supported by citations to literature on acidopore grooming behavior.

claim: Acidopore grooming is a specialized behavior existing only in a subset of ant families among all Hymenopterans.
source: during a specialized behavior existing only in a subset of ant families among all Hymenopterans (Basibuyuk and Quicke, 1999; Farish, 1972), termed acidopore grooming.
evidence: Supported by citations to literature on the phylogenetic distribution of acidopore grooming.

claim: The ensuing acidic environment in the stomach, the crop, can limit the establishment of pathogenic and opportunistic microbes ingested with food.
source: The ensuing acidic environment in the stomach, the crop, can limit the establishment of pathogenic and opportunistic microbes ingested with food
evidence: Supported by experimental data from bacterial viability and survival experiments.

claim: Crop acidity can improve the survival of ants when faced with pathogen contaminated food.
source: and improve the survival of ants when faced with pathogen contaminated food.
evidence: Supported by survival experiment data.

claim: Crop acidity selectively allows acquisition and colonization by Acetobacteraceae.
source: At the same time, crop acidity selectively allows acquisition and colonization by Acetobacteraceae, known bacterial gut associates of formicine ants.
evidence: Supported by differential bacterial survival data for Asaia sp. versus pathogenic bacteria.

claim: Swallowing of the poison in formicine ants acts as a microbial filter.
source: This suggests that swallowing of the poison in formicine ants acts as a microbial filter
evidence: Conclusion inferred from differential bacterial survival and passage data.

claim: Antimicrobials have a potentially widespread but so far underappreciated dual role in host-microbe interactions.
source: and that antimicrobials have a potentially widespread but so far underappreciated dual role in host-microbe interactions.
evidence: Speculative conclusion about broader implications of the findings.

claim: The midgut is the primary site of digestion in insects.
source: the midgut, the primary site of digestion in insects (Holtof et al., 2019; Terra and Ferreira, 1994
evidence: Supported by citations to literature on insect digestive physiology.

claim: Serratia marcescens is an insect pathogenic bacterium.
source: As model entomopathogenic bacterium Serratia marcescens DSM12481 (DSMZ Braunschweig, Germany) was used. This bacterium is pathogenic in a range of insects (Grimont and Grimont, 2006)
evidence: Supported by citation to literature on S. marcescens pathogenicity.

claim: Serratia marcescens has been detected in formicine ants Anoplolepis gracilipes and Camponotus floridanus.
source: and has been detected in formicine ants, that is Anoplolepis gracilipes (Cooling et al., 2018) and Camponotus floridanus (Ratzka et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to literature on S. marcescens detection in ants.

claim: S. marcescens can cross the insect gut wall.
source: While often non-lethal within the digestive tract, S. marcescens can cross the insect gut wall (Mirabito and Rosengaus, 2016; Nehme et al., 2007)
evidence: Supported by citations to literature on S. marcescens infection mechanisms.

claim: S. marcescens is highly virulent upon entry into the hemocoel, not least due to the production of bacterial toxins.
source: and is highly virulent upon entry into the hemocoel (Flyg et al., 1980), not least due to the production of bacterial toxins (Hertle, 2005).
evidence: Supported by citations to literature on S. marcescens virulence and toxin production.

claim: Asaia sp. belongs to the family Acetobacteraceae, members of which often thrive in sugar-rich environments.
source: Asaia sp. belongs to the family Acetobacteraceae, members of which often thrive in sugar-rich environments (Mamlouk and Gullo, 2013), such as honeydew that ants like C. floridanus predominantly feed on.
evidence: Supported by citation to literature on Acetobacteraceae ecology.

claim: Asaia sp. is capable of cross-colonizing insects of phylogenetically distant genera and orders.
source: Asaia sp. is capable of cross-colonizing insects of phylogenetically distant genera and orders (Crotti et al., 2009; Favia et al., 2007)
evidence: Supported by citations to literature on Asaia sp. host range.

claim: Asaia sp. can be a component of the gut-associated microbial community of formicine and other ants.
source: and can be a component of the gut-associated microbial community of formicine and other ants (Chua et al., 2018; Kautz et al., 2013a; Kautz et al., 2013b).
evidence: Supported by citations to literature on Asaia sp. in ant microbiomes.

claim: E. coli bacteria are a principal constituent of mammalian gut-associated microbial communities but are commonly also found in the environment.
source: E. coli bacteria are a principal constituent of mammalian gut-associated microbial communities but are commonly also found in the environment (Blount, 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to literature on E. coli ecology.

claim: In ants, gut morphological structures consecutively filter solid particles down to 2 µm.
source: In ants, gut morphological structures, that is, the infrabuccal pocket, an invagination of the hypopharynx in the oral cavity (Eisner and Happ, 1962), and the proventriculus, a valve that mechanically restricts passage of fluids from the crop to the midgut (Eisner and Wilson, 1952), consecutively filter solid particles down to 2 µm (Lanan et al., 2016)
evidence: Supported by citations to literature on ant gut morphology and particle filtration.
